Subject: Sizing ask: pilot throughput + latency constraints

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the team is keen to move to a small paid pilot. Before we lock dates we need a practical sizing recommendation for Dedicated capacity that meets our SLOs. TL;DR of our workload: average 900 tokens per call (open-ended assistant), expected steady-state traffic 18 req/s with short bursts to 60 req/s during business hours, typical request pattern is many short chats (1–3 turns) plus occasional long-form generations.

Key SLO: p95 response time <= 250ms for interactive responses (we understand very long generations will be higher).

Questions:
- For model family: we plan to use rw-instruct-7b or rw-instruct-13b quantized variants — what dedicated GPU count should we reserve to guarantee the SLO at steady and burst?
- What headroom do you recommend for a 90-day pilot?
- Any quick levers (caching, batching, model variant) we should use to reduce committed footprint?

I attached a CSV with our estimated token distribution by endpoint (nimbus_token_profile.csv). Can you provide a short proposal and an estimated monthly commitment?

Thanks,
Sara

Hi Sara — great to hear the pilot is moving forward. Appreciate the CSV; I skimmed it and pasted a few initial numbers below. Ben and Priyom are looped in to validate the perf math.

Initial high-level recommendation (rough estimates):
- Steady-state: reserve a small Dedicated slab equivalent to 8x A100-80GB-class instances (we'll translate to our SKU matrix). That maps to ~720k tokens/sec aggregate capacity under our optimized runtime for rw-instruct-7b-q4_0, or ~420k tokens/sec for rw-instruct-13b-q4_0 (quantized).
- Burst: allow auto-burst up to 24 GPUs (3x the reserved slab) for 6–8 hours/day for launch spikes.
- Headroom: recommend 25–30% operational headroom for the first 90 days while caching and prompt templates are tuned.

Levers we will apply: prefix KV caching for repeated short chats, request-level batching below 30ms to preserve latency, and recommending rw-instruct-7b for interactive endpoints where quality trade is acceptable.

I'll ask Ben/Priyom to run a tokens/sec -> GPUs mapping with your token distribution and target p95 latency so we can convert to an explicit commit + burst and produce a short PDF proposal. Would you be open to a 30-minute sizing call Thursday?

Ben / Priyom — forwarding Nimbus' profile. Quick ask: can you validate the numbers below and return a short calc sheet we can send to Sara? Important constraints: p95 <= 250ms, steady 18 req/s (900 tokens avg), bursts to 60 req/s (same token avg). Their mix: ~70% short chats (single-turn after priming), 20% multi-turn small (2–4 turns), 10% long-form (>=2k tokens).

My back-of-envelope: 8 GPUs reserved (rw7b-q4) -> ~720k tokens/sec seems optimistic; I'd rather quote based on realistic tokens/sec per GPU numbers from our bench:
- rw-instruct-7b-q4_0: ~90k tokens/sec per A100-80GB-like GPU (online, 1 concurrent stream per device)
- rw-instruct-13b-q4_0: ~52k tokens/sec per GPU

If these hold, for steady 18 req/s * 900 tokens = 16,200 tokens/sec -> ~0.18 GPUs (so steady is very small). Bursts at 60 req/s -> 54,000 tokens/sec -> ~0.6 GPUs (13b footprint larger). Obviously concurrency, KV cache miss penalties, and latency budget change the mapping — so please produce two scenarios (conservative and optimistic) and call out assumptions. Also include an ops playbook: warm cache, pre-warming burst, graceful degradation to 7b if 13b latency rises.

Thanks — can you turn around by EOD?

Kim
From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>

Kim / Priyom — quick compute notes and recommended commit. I validated against our perf bench for the rw-instruct family with standard prompt lengths. Assumptions: 8-bit quantized kernels, single-stream interactive mode, average sequence length during generation 900 tokens, target tail latency budget p95 <= 250ms (this budget excludes extremely long-form >2k token jobs where we recommend async).

Bench results (median across hardware sku mapping):
- rw-instruct-7b-q4_0: ~85k tokens/sec per GPU (p50); tail (p95) safe sustained throughput ~55k tokens/sec per GPU when preserving <250ms for typical short-turn responses.
- rw-instruct-13b-q4_0: ~48k tokens/sec per GPU (p50); tail safe sustained ~30k tokens/sec per GPU for p95 <250ms.

Sizing math (conservative tail figures):
- Steady demand: 18 req/s * 900 tokens = 16,200 t/s -> fits on 1 GPU comfortably (both models), but this ignores concurrent long-form jobs and KV cold misses.
- Burst peak: 60 req/s * 900 = 54,000 t/s -> for p95 preservation:
    * 7b -> 54,000 / 55,000 ~= 1.0 GPUs (conservative)
    * 13b -> 54,000 / 30,000 ~= 1.8 -> round to 2 GPUs

Recommendation:
- Commit slab: reserve 4 GPUs as a conservative pilot commit (covers steady + concurrent long-jobs + room for 2–3 engineers stress testing). This is a small committed tier that keeps contract minimal while giving us predictable throughput.
- Burst: allow auto-burst up to 16 GPUs (4x) for launch windows and simulated traffic runs. This is cheaper than a heavy commit and gives Nimbus room to ramp.
- Headroom: 30% buffer for KV cold misses and orchestration variance.

Operational levers to reduce commit:
- Aggressive prefix KV caching reduces cold-path token work by ~35% for their 70% short-chat mix.
- Recommend routing short interactive endpoints to 7b at the edge and reserving 13b for long-form where quality is critical.

I'll attach quick notes (compute-math-notes.txt) and an exportable tab of the calc. If agreed, we should produce a one-page commercial proposal with commit = 4 GPUs, burst up to 16, 30% headroom, 6-week ramp schedule, and an option to convert to 8 GPU commit after month 2 if utilization justifies it.

Ben
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
